rw: Admitting a real weakness and showing the steps you take to improve it shows honesty and self-awareness, which is what interviewers want to see.

ww.Name a weakness that makes you unfit for: Naming a flaw that makes you unfit for the job hurts your chances, because it gives the employer a direct reason to reject you.
ww.Refuse to answer the question and move o: Refusing to answer looks evasive and uncooperative, and it wastes a chance to show maturity, so the interviewer will likely mark you down for it.
ww.Say you have no weaknesses at all in any: Claiming no weaknesses at all sounds untruthful or lacking self-awareness, since everyone has areas to improve, and interviewers tend to distrust that kind of answer.

rw: A job offer is the employer's formal proposal to hire you, stating terms such as pay, duties and start date, which you can then accept or decline.

ww.A job advertisement posted on a board or: A job advertisement only invites people to apply and describes an open position, so it comes before any offer and does not hire anyone by itself.
ww.A rejection letter sent to an applicant: A rejection letter tells an applicant they were not chosen, which is the opposite of an offer, since an offer proposes to hire the person.
ww.A request from you to leave a job, hande: A written request to leave a job is a resignation notice sent by the worker to the manager, so it comes from you instead of the employer.

rw: Reviewing pay, benefits, duties and schedule lets you confirm the job meets your needs and money goals before you commit, which is the sensible way to judge an offer.

ww.Only how close it is to a friend: Distance to a friend is not a reason to judge a job, and looking at one personal detail ignores the pay, duties and hours that decide fit.
ww.Nothing, as all offers are the same: Offers differ widely in pay, benefits, duties and hours, so claiming all offers are the same would lead you to accept a poor deal without checking.
ww.Only the color of the office walls: Office wall color has almost no bearing on your income or daily work, so judging an offer by it ignores the terms that truly matter to you.

rw: A notice of resignation is the message you send to tell your employer you are leaving, usually giving advance warning so they can plan for your absence.

ww.A message firing you from the job that y: A message that fires you is a termination notice sent by the employer, while a resignation notice is written by the employee who has chosen to leave.
ww.A message about your pay sent by a firm: A monthly message about pay is a pay stub or statement from the firm, which reports earnings and has nothing to do with quitting the job.
ww.A message offering you a job, sent after: A message offering you a job after an interview is a job offer from the employer, which is the reverse of a notice you send to leave.

rw: The law of demand says that as price rises, the quantity buyers want falls, and that is exactly why the bakery sells fewer muffins after raising its price.

ww.The law of supply: The law of supply says higher prices lead sellers to offer more, but here the key result is that buyers purchase fewer muffins, which is demand behavior.
ww.Inflation of prices: Inflation means prices rise across the whole economy over time, while this bakery raised only its own muffin price and saw sales respond, which is not general inflation.
ww.Opportunity cost: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best option given up when choosing, and the bakery example shows buyers reacting to price, not weighing a forgone choice.

rw: When demand grows and supply stays the same, buyers compete for the limited stock, so sellers can charge more and the price usually rises.

ww.It is flat: Prices do not stay flat when more people want the same fixed supply, because shoppers compete for the limited sneakers and push the price upward.
ww.It hits zero: A price falling to zero would mean the sneaker became free, which makes no sense when more people want it and the supply has not grown.
ww.It falls: A falling price happens when demand drops or supply grows, but here demand increased with supply unchanged, so the pressure pushes the price up instead.

rw: With far more apples for the same number of buyers, sellers must lower prices to sell the extra supply, so the price usually falls.

ww.It doubles: A price doubling would need demand to surge or supply to shrink, but here supply grew a lot while demand held steady, which pushes the price down.
ww.It rises: A rising price would follow from scarcity or higher demand, whereas here a large crop means plenty of apples for the same buyers, so the price drops.
ww.Fixed by law: A price fixed by law is a price control, which is not what normally happens in a market when supply simply increases, so it does not answer the question.

rw: A substitute good is one that can replace another, so buyers switch to it when the first good gets expensive, such as tea in place of coffee.

ww.A product used together with another: Products used together are complement goods, such as bread and butter, which is the opposite idea from a substitute that takes the place of another.
ww.A product made in another country: Where a product is made, whether in another country or at home, does not decide whether it is a substitute, which depends on whether buyers can swap it.
ww.A product that no one wants to buy: A product no one wants has no demand at all, and that says nothing about whether it can stand in for another good.

rw: A complement good is used together with another good, so demand for one rises and falls with the other, like printers and ink.

ww.A product sold at a discount price: Selling at a discount describes a pricing choice and not a relationship between two goods, so it does not define what a complement good is.
ww.A product that replaces another one: A product that replaces another is a substitute good, which is the opposite of a complement, since complements are bought together.
ww.A product that is free to all buyers: Being free to all buyers has nothing to do with complements, because a complement can carry a normal price while still being used with another good.

rw: Hot dogs and buns are used together, so they are complements, and when hot dogs get pricier people buy fewer of them and also fewer buns.

ww.It stays the same in price and in sales: Demand for buns would not hold steady, since people who buy fewer hot dogs after the price rise will need fewer buns to go with them.
ww.It becomes impossible to measure at all: Demand for buns can be measured easily, by counting how many buns are bought at each price of hot dogs, so saying it is impossible is false.
ww.It rises, because the goods are substitu: Substitutes would show demand rising when the other good gets pricier, but buns do not replace hot dogs, they go with them, so demand falls.

rw: A trade-off means giving up one thing to get another, because resources like time and money are limited and each choice has a cost.

ww.A tax on traded goods and gems: A tax on traded goods is a tariff or duty, which is a different idea from a trade-off, where you give up one option to gain another.
ww.Getting both choices free at no cost: Getting both choices free would mean no cost at all, but a trade-off exists because choosing one thing means giving up another, so a cost always remains.
ww.A swap of money between two banks: A money swap between banks is a financial transfer and not a choice between two options, so it does not describe a trade-off.

rw: Economic growth is an increase in a country's total output of goods and services over time, which usually means more jobs and higher incomes.

ww.A fall in the number of workers over yea: A fall in the number of workers would usually shrink output instead of increasing it, so it signals decline and not economic growth.
ww.A rise in the size of a store or a shop: One shop getting bigger is business growth in a single firm, while economic growth measures output across a whole country, so the two are different.
ww.A rise in the price of goods for buyers: A rise in prices is inflation, which says nothing about producing more, since prices can climb even when a country's output is flat or falling.

rw: The business cycle is the repeating pattern of expansion and contraction in the economy, with periods of growth followed by slowdowns and then recovery.

ww.The path a product takes to a customer f: The path a product takes from factory to customer is the supply chain or distribution channel, which is a different idea from the business cycle.
ww.A bike route in a city that riders use t: A bike route for riders is a transport matter and is unrelated to economics, even though the word cycle appears in the name.
ww.A store's yearly sales calendar listing: A store's yearly sales calendar tracks that single shop's promotion dates, and not the economy wide swings in output and jobs that the business cycle describes.

rw: In an expansion the economy grows, so firms produce more, hire more workers and incomes tend to rise across the country.

ww.Businesses stop producing goods here: Businesses stopping production describes a deep downturn and not an expansion, because during expansion firms usually make more goods and not fewer.
ww.Prices are fixed by law for all goods: Prices fixed by law is a price control policy, which is unrelated to expansion, and in an expansion prices are mostly set by markets.
ww.Output, jobs and income all fall: Falling output, jobs and income describes a contraction or recession, which is the opposite of an expansion, when the economy is growing.

rw: A recession is a period of economic decline, so output and jobs tend to fall as firms sell less and cut back on hiring.

ww.Banks give away money to all: Banks giving away money to all is not what happens in a recession, when lenders usually become more cautious and lend less, not more.
ww.Output and jobs rise quickly: Output and jobs rising quickly describes an expansion or boom, the opposite of a recession, in which production slows and firms cut staff.
ww.Prices stop existing for goods: Prices keep existing in a recession, since goods are still bought and sold, so saying prices stop existing is plainly untrue.

rw: A standard of living is the level of comfort, goods and services people have in a place, shown by things like housing, income and healthcare.

ww.The number of people in a house, divided: People per room is a measure of crowding, which is only one small detail of housing and does not capture the full standard of living.
ww.The cost of a single home that a family: The cost of one home is a single price and not a measure of how well people live overall, so it does not define the term.
ww.The size of a city measured by the peopl: City size by population is a measure of how big a place is, but a big city can have a high or low standard of living, so it does not define it.

rw: Specialization means focusing on making a few goods or doing a few tasks, which lets people and firms become more skilled and efficient at them.

ww.Buying goods from many countries to give: Buying goods from many countries is international trade and gives shoppers variety, which differs from specialization, where a worker or firm focuses on a few goods.
ww.Making every product yourself with no he: Making every product yourself with no help is self sufficiency, which is the opposite of specialization, where people rely on others for what they do not make.
ww.Hiring workers without skills and giving: Hiring unskilled workers with no training does not describe specialization, which depends on workers building skill in a narrow task, not lacking skill.

rw: Focusing on one task lets workers practice it often, so they get faster and more skilled, which raises how much they can produce.

ww.They make more mistakes as they grow bor: Making more mistakes from boredom would lower productivity, so it cannot explain why specialization raises it, since specialized workers actually improve through repetition.
ww.They work fewer hours for the same pay e: Working fewer hours for the same pay is not the reason, because productivity means producing more output, not simply working less time.
ww.They avoid learning new things at their: Avoiding learning new things would not raise productivity, since specialized workers actually build deep skill in their task and so they do learn.

rw: Money is anything widely accepted as payment for goods and services, which can be coins, notes or digital balances as long as people accept it.

ww.Only credit cards and debit cards used i: Credit and debit cards are only one way to pay, and cash and other forms of money count as well, so the word only makes this too narrow.
ww.Only things you can touch, such as coins: Coins and banknotes are physical money, but money also exists in digital forms like bank balances, so limiting it to things you can touch is too narrow.
ww.Only gold bars held in a vault by a bank: Gold bars in a vault may have value, but money does not have to be gold, and modern money rests on general acceptance, so the word only is wrong.

rw: Barter is trading goods or services directly for other goods or services, with no money used, such as swapping eggs for bread.

ww.Selling goods for cash at a shop to buye: Selling goods for cash at a shop uses money, but barter works with no money at all, so this does not describe it.
ww.Buying goods with a credit card and payi: Buying with a credit card and paying later is a use of credit, and it still involves money, which barter avoids entirely.
ww.Paying taxes to the government each year: Paying taxes is a duty to the government paid in money, which has nothing to do with swapping goods or services directly.

rw: An economy is a system for producing, distributing and using goods and services, which links households, firms and government in a region or country.

ww.A list of laws passed by a government in: A list of laws passed in one year is a legislative record and does not explain how goods and services are made and shared, which is what an economy is.
ww.A bank that lends money to firms and to: A bank is one financial institution that lends money, and it is only one part of an economy, so it cannot be the whole thing.
ww.A store that sells cheap goods to the pu: A discount store is one business among many, so it is only a small part of an economy and not the whole system of production and trade.

rw: A monopoly has just one seller and no close substitutes, so buyers have nowhere else to turn and the seller has strong power over price.

ww.A market with two sellers and very many: A market with two sellers is a duopoly, not a monopoly, and having very many buyers does not change that more than one seller exists.
ww.A market with no buyers and very many se: A market needs buyers to exist at all, so one with no buyers is not a monopoly, which is defined by having a single seller.
ww.A market with many sellers of similar go: A market with many sellers of similar goods describes competition, which is the opposite of a monopoly, where one seller controls supply.

rw: Businesses exist to provide goods or services that meet people's needs and to earn a profit, which rewards owners and keeps the firm running.

ww.To collect donations from people who wis: Collecting donations is the work of charities, while most businesses exist to sell goods or services to customers and earn money from those sales.
ww.To remove competition from the market an: Businesses exist to serve customers, and removing competition to set high prices is a harmful goal that is often illegal, not the basic reason firms exist.
ww.To avoid paying taxes to the state on an: Avoiding taxes is not why businesses exist, and a firm that earns income generally must pay taxes under the law like everyone else.

rw: A nonprofit uses its income to pursue a mission instead of paying owners, so surplus money goes back into its work rather than to private shareholders.

ww.An organization that loses money on purp: Nonprofits do not aim to lose money on purpose, because they need to cover costs to keep running, and they often charge fees or sell things too.
ww.An organization that never earns revenue: Nonprofits can earn revenue from fees, sales and grants as well as gifts, so saying they never earn revenue is false, though they do not pay owners.
ww.An organization owned by shareholders wh: An organization owned by shareholders who share profits is a for-profit corporation, which is the reverse of a nonprofit that has no owners to pay.

rw: The private sector is the part of the economy owned by individuals and companies, as opposed to the government, and it works to earn profit.

ww.The part that is hidden from public view: Hidden from public view is not what private sector means, since private firms still follow laws and keep records, and the term is about ownership.
ww.The part owned by charities only, funded: Charities alone do not make up the private sector, which also includes the many ordinary profit seeking businesses that individuals and companies own.
ww.The part run by the government and its a: The part run by the government is the public sector, which is the opposite of the private sector owned by people and companies.

rw: The public sector is the part of the economy run by government, including services such as public schools, roads and the military.

ww.The part owned by foreign firms only: Foreign owned firms can belong to the private sector, so ownership by foreigners does not define the public sector, which is about government control.
ww.The part that sells stock to the public: Selling stock to the public is something private corporations do to raise money, so it describes a type of firm and not the government run public sector.
ww.The part owned and run by private firms: Private firms owned and run by individuals make up the private sector, which is the opposite of the public sector run by government.

rw: An employee performs work for a business and receives pay in exchange, which is the basic role that separates employees from owners and customers.

ww.To supply raw materials to the firm: Supplying raw materials is the job of suppliers, not employees, who work inside the firm instead of selling inputs to it.
ww.To own the company and run it alone: Owning and running a company alone describes a sole owner, and employees do not own the firm, they work for it under the owner.
ww.To buy the company's products only: Buying the company's products only describes a customer, whereas an employee works for the firm and does not simply purchase from it.

rw: Entrepreneurship means starting and running a business while accepting the risk of loss, in the hope of earning a profit from a new idea.

ww.Working for a large firm and taking orde: Working for a large firm and taking orders is being an employee, which carries little personal risk, so it differs from the risk taking of entrepreneurship.
ww.Avoiding all risk by taking a job with a: Avoiding risk by taking a fixed pay job is the opposite of entrepreneurship, because entrepreneurs accept uncertain income and the chance of failure.
ww.Investing only in stocks, bonds and fund: Investing only in stocks and bonds is a form of investing, and it does not involve starting and running a business, which defines entrepreneurship.

rw: Business owners put their own money into the firm, so if it fails they can lose that investment, which is a real financial risk of ownership.

ww.Guaranteed profit in every year of tradi: A guaranteed profit every year does not exist for business owners, so it cannot be a risk, and it describes a benefit that is untrue.
ww.No need to work hard to run the business: Having no need to work hard is not a risk of ownership, and owners usually work very hard, so this option is unrealistic.
ww.Freedom from all competition, as new fir: Freedom from all competition is not a risk but would be an advantage if true, and new firms usually face rivals rather than owning the market.

rw: A stakeholder is anyone affected by a business's decisions, including owners, workers, customers, suppliers and the community around it.

ww.Only the government and its agencies: The government is only one possible stakeholder, and the word only leaves out customers, workers and owners who are also affected by a firm's decisions.
ww.Only the competitors of the business: Competitors may be affected, but they are not the only stakeholders, since workers, customers and owners are also affected, so the word only makes it wrong.
ww.Only the owner, as no one else is affect: Owners are stakeholders, but others such as employees, customers and neighbors are affected by the business too, so saying only the owner is false.

rw: Social responsibility means acting in ways that benefit society and the environment, and not only the owners, such as reducing pollution and treating workers fairly.

ww.A business avoiding all rules that apply: Avoiding all rules is the opposite of social responsibility, because responsible firms follow laws and often go beyond them to benefit others.
ww.A business ignoring its community and th: Ignoring the community and its needs is the reverse of social responsibility, which means caring about the people and places a business affects.
ww.A business raising prices on everyone to: Raising prices on everyone to pay for green projects is a particular pricing choice and not the definition, which is about acting for the good of society.

rw: Reducing waste and supporting local charities benefits the environment and the community, which fits the idea of acting for society and not only for profit.

ww.A company dumping waste in a river to sa: Dumping waste in a river harms the environment and the people nearby just to save cost, so it is irresponsible and often illegal.
ww.A company hiding safety problems from it: Hiding safety problems from customers and staff puts people at risk and breaks trust, so it is the opposite of responsible behavior.
ww.A company ignoring complaints from custo: Ignoring complaints from customers and staff shows disregard for the people the firm affects, so it is not an example of social responsibility.

rw: Business ethics is the set of principles about right and wrong that guide how companies and their people behave, such as honesty and fairness.

ww.Rules for filing taxes with the state ea: Rules for filing taxes belong to tax law and accounting, which are legal requirements and not the moral principles that business ethics refers to.
ww.A list of company products and their pri: A list of products and prices is a catalog or price list, which describes goods for sale and has nothing to do with right and wrong.
ww.A schedule of employee shifts, posted in: A schedule of employee shifts is a work roster for managing staff time, which is not about moral principles in how a business behaves.

rw: Knowingly selling a defective product puts buyers in danger and breaks both moral standards and often safety laws, so it is unethical and possibly illegal.

ww.A normal practice in most cases: Selling a known unsafe product is not normal practice, and it risks harm to buyers and legal trouble for the seller, so it is not accepted behavior.
ww.A required procedure for staff: No firm requires staff to sell products they know are dangerous, and doing so is not a procedure but a wrongful act that breaks safety rules.
ww.Good customer service for buyers: Good service means treating customers well and protecting them, so knowingly selling a dangerous product is the opposite and cannot count as good service.

rw: A brand is a name, symbol or design that identifies a company's products and sets them apart from rivals in the minds of customers.

ww.A store's address and the phone number o: A store's address and phone number are contact details that help customers find the shop, but they do not make up a brand.
ww.The tax on a product that a buyer pays a: A tax paid at the till is a sales tax charged by the government, which is unrelated to the name or symbol that identifies a product.
ww.The cost of making a product, including: The cost of making a product is its production cost, an accounting figure that says nothing about how a company's products are identified.

rw: Reputation is how customers and the public view a business, based on its past behavior, quality and service, and it affects who chooses to buy from it.

ww.The size of a store or a shop in a town: The size of a store is a physical feature of the shop, while reputation is about how people view the business, so size does not define it.
ww.The money kept in a bank account of the: Money in a bank account is a financial asset of the firm, which is separate from the opinion people hold about the business.
ww.The number of employees of the firm in a: The number of employees measures the firm's staff size, which tells you nothing about what customers and the public think of the business.

rw: A traditional economy decides what to make and how to share it by following customs and traditions passed down through generations, often in farming or hunting societies.

ww.Market economy only: A market economy relies on buyers and sellers making choices through competition and prices, not on customs and traditions, so this does not fit.
ww.Command economy only: A command economy has the government make the main decisions through central plans, which is different from relying on custom and tradition.
ww.Mixed economy type: A mixed economy blends market choices with government direction, and it is not mainly guided by customs, so it is not the system described.

rw: Competition among businesses for customers is typical of a market economy, because many sellers try to win buyers with better prices and quality.

ww.No private ownership of any goods or fir: No private ownership of goods or firms describes a fully state controlled system and not a market economy, which depends on private ownership.
ww.A single plan set by the state for firms: A single plan set by the state for firms is typical of a command economy, which is the opposite of a market where firms make their own choices.
ww.Jobs fixed by custom from the day of bir: Jobs fixed by custom from birth are typical of a traditional economy, where roles pass down by family, and not of a market economy with free choice.

rw: Planners decide for everyone without price signals, so they may fail to know what people want, leading to shortages of some goods and surpluses of others.

ww.Consumers choose too many goods that pla: In a command economy planners choose what is made, so consumers cannot choose too many goods, and this describes a market feature and not a weakness of planning.
ww.Prices rise and fall too freely in the m: Prices rising and falling freely in a market is how a market economy works, whereas command economies usually have prices set by planners, so it is not their weakness.
ww.Too many businesses compete for the buye: Many businesses competing for buyers is a mark of a market economy, but a command economy has few or no competing firms, so this is not its weakness.

rw: A purely free market has little government help, so people with little money may be unable to afford basic needs, which is a real weakness.

ww.No competition exists in the market: Competition is a feature of a free market and not an absent one, so claiming no competition exists describes a monopoly or a command system.
ww.Customs control every choice: Customs controlling every choice describes a traditional economy, not a free market, where individuals and firms make their own choices.
ww.The government decides every price: The government deciding every price describes a command economy, whereas in a free market prices come from supply and demand.

rw: A public good is one everyone can use, and no one can easily be excluded from it, such as national defense, which is shared by all citizens.

ww.A product sold in stores to the public d: A product sold in stores to the public is just an ordinary private good that buyers purchase, and it is not what economists mean by a public good.
ww.A product used up by one person at one t: A product used up by one person at one time is a private good, since public goods can be used by many without being used up.
ww.A product only the wealthy can buy, sold: A product only the wealthy can buy describes a luxury good, whereas a public good is open for everyone to use, not just those with high incomes.

rw: Because users of public goods are hard to charge, private firms may not profit from providing them, so the government supplies them using tax money.

ww.Public goods always lose money by law, s: Public goods do not lose money by any law, and the reason firms avoid them is that collecting payment is hard, not that a rule forces losses.
ww.Private firms are banned from making goo: Private firms are not banned from making goods, and some public goods like fireworks shows or roads can involve private firms, so this reason is false.
ww.Citizens refuse to use private goods, an: Citizens do use private goods freely, and the actual reason the state provides public goods is that markets under supply them, not that people refuse private ones.

rw: A tax is a required payment to the government, used to fund public services such as roads, schools and defense.

ww.A voluntary gift to charity by a person: A voluntary gift to charity is a donation made by choice, whereas a tax is required by law, so the two are different things.
ww.A fee for a private service paid: A fee for a private service is a price paid to a business, not to the government, so it does not describe a tax.
ww.A loan from the government to buyers: A loan from the government to buyers is a form of credit that must be repaid, while a tax is a payment that people make to the government.

rw: Public roads are shared by everyone and paid for mostly by taxes collected by the government, which build and maintain them for public use.

ww.A movie ticket: A movie ticket is bought by the person who attends the show and paid to a private business, not funded mainly by taxes.
ww.A meal out: A meal out is paid for by the diner to a private restaurant, so taxes do not mainly pay for it.
ww.New sneakers: New sneakers are a private good that the buyer pays for directly in a store, so taxes do not mostly fund them.

rw: Regulation means government rules that businesses must follow, such as safety, labor and environmental standards, meant to protect the public and keep markets fair.

ww.A tax on profits paid by firms to the st: A tax on profits paid by firms is corporate income tax, which raises money for the state, whereas regulation sets rules for how firms behave.
ww.A business's own plan for its sales and: A business's own plan for sales and costs is a budget or business plan made by the firm, not a rule set by government.
ww.Money given to firms by the state to hel: Money given to firms by the state to help growth is a subsidy, which supports businesses, whereas regulation limits or directs what they do.

map.To help one company win: To help one company win over its rivals
map.A job title that is printed on the card: To let sellers hide unsafe food from buyers

rw: Food safety rules exist to protect consumers from harm such as contamination and illness, since buyers cannot easily check how safe their food is themselves.

ww.To raise the price of food: Raising the price of food is not the purpose of food safety rules, which aim to keep food safe, and they are not meant to push prices up.
ww.To help one company win over its rivals: Helping one company beat its rivals is not the purpose of safety rules, which apply to all food sellers equally and aim to protect the public.
ww.To let sellers hide unsafe food from buy: Letting sellers hide unsafe food would put buyers at risk, so it is the opposite of what food safety regulation is designed to do.

rw: Variable cost is 250 items times $4, which is $1,000, and adding the $1,000 fixed cost gives a total cost of $2,000.

ww.$1,250: The figure $1,250 comes from adding $1,000 to only $250, which treats each item as costing $1, but the variable cost is $4 per item.
ww.$1,004: The figure $1,004 adds the $1,000 fixed cost to a single item's $4 variable cost, but the shop makes 250 items, so variable cost is $1,000.
ww.$4,000: The figure $4,000 multiplies $4 by 1,000, which mixes up the fixed cost with the item count, while the right math is $1,000 plus 250 times $4.

rw: The break even point is the sales level where revenue equals total costs, so the business makes neither profit nor loss at that level.

ww.The point where sales are zero for the y: Zero sales for the year would mean no revenue at all, so the firm would be losing its fixed costs, which is not the break even point.
ww.The point where costs are zero for the f: Costs are not zero for a working firm, since it must pay for materials, wages and rent, so this cannot be the break even point.
ww.The point where profit is highest, after: The point of highest profit is a different idea, because break even is where profit is exactly zero, not where it is largest.

rw: Break even equals fixed costs divided by earnings per item, so $600 divided by $3 gives 200 items, and 200 times $3 covers the $600 exactly.

ww.180 items: The figure 180 items would give only $540 in earnings above variable cost at $3 each, which is less than the $600 fixed costs, so it falls short.
ww.1,800 items: The figure 1,800 items looks like a slip by a factor of ten, since 1,800 times $3 is $5,400, far more than the $600 needed.
ww.600 items: The figure 600 items treats the fixed cost as a count and ignores the $3 per item, whereas 600 times $3 is $1,800, far beyond what is needed.

rw: Gross profit is sales minus the cost of goods sold, which shows how much a firm earns from selling products before other expenses.

ww.Sales minus all expenses and taxes: Sales minus all expenses and taxes is net profit, which subtracts more than gross profit does, since gross profit only subtracts cost of goods sold.
ww.Assets minus liabilities of a firm: Assets minus liabilities is a firm's equity or net worth from its balance sheet, which is a measure of ownership value and not a profit figure.
ww.Sales plus the cost of goods sold: Adding cost of goods sold to sales gives a meaningless number larger than sales, while gross profit comes from subtracting that cost.

rw: Gross profit is sales minus cost of goods sold, so $20,000 minus $12,000 equals $8,000.

ww.$20,000: The figure $20,000 is just the sales amount and ignores subtracting the $12,000 cost of goods sold, so it overstates the gross profit.
ww.$32,000: The figure $32,000 comes from adding sales and cost of goods sold, but gross profit requires subtracting, which gives $8,000 instead.
ww.$12,000: The figure $12,000 is only the cost of goods sold, not the profit, since the profit is what remains after taking that cost from $20,000.

rw: Net profit is the money left after subtracting all expenses and taxes from revenue, making it the final measure of how much the business earned.

ww.Sales before any costs are paid out by u: Sales before any costs are paid is revenue or gross sales, which is the starting amount and not what remains as profit.
ww.Sales minus the cost of the goods made: Sales minus the cost of the goods made is gross profit, which leaves out other expenses and taxes that net profit also subtracts.
ww.The value of what the business owns at y: The value of what the business owns is its assets, which come from the balance sheet and are not the same as earnings for the year.

rw: Overhead is the ongoing cost of running a business, such as rent and utilities, which does not change with how much of any one product is made.

ww.The cost of materials in a product that: Materials that rise with the number made are variable costs, which change with output, whereas overhead stays about the same however many units are produced.
ww.The profit of the owner after all costs: The owner's profit after all costs is net income, which is what is left after costs, and overhead is itself one of those costs.
ww.The pay of workers who make the product,: Pay for workers who make the product rises with units made, so it is a direct labor cost, not overhead, which is not tied to one product.

rw: A budget is a plan for income and spending, which helps people and businesses control costs and make sure money is available when needed.

ww.A record of past sales over years: A record of past sales is a sales history report, which looks backward, while a budget is a plan that looks ahead at income and spending.
ww.A list of customers and addresses: A list of customers and addresses is a mailing or customer list, which has nothing to do with planning how money will be earned and spent.
ww.A tax return filed each year: A tax return is a form filed with the government to report income and tax, not a plan for future spending, so it is not a budget.

rw: Tracking costs closely lets a new business keep spending below revenue, so it stays profitable and avoids losses that could force it to close.

ww.To raise costs on purpose each month of: Raising costs on purpose each month would hurt the business, so no smart owner would track costs for that reason.
ww.To make the business look bigger to bank: Tracking costs gives a true picture of finances, and making a firm look bigger than it is would be misleading to banks, so it is not the goal.
ww.To avoid paying anyone for their work or: Avoiding payment to people for their work is unfair and often illegal, and tracking costs is meant to manage money, not to dodge obligations.

rw: A discount is a reduction in the price of a product, which lets buyers pay less than the normal amount for the same item.

ww.A fee for shipping goods to a buyer: A fee for shipping goods is a delivery charge that adds to what a buyer pays, whereas a discount lowers the price.
ww.An increase in the price of a product: An increase in the price of a product is a markup or price rise, which is the opposite of a discount that lowers the price.
ww.A tax on a sale of goods in a shop: A tax on a sale is a sales tax, which adds to the total the buyer pays, whereas a discount takes money off.

rw: Twenty percent of $50 is $10, and subtracting that from $50 leaves a sale price of $40.

ww.$30: The figure $30 would be a 40 percent discount, since $50 minus $30 is $20 off, but 20 percent of $50 is only $10 off.
ww.$10: The figure $10 is the amount taken off, being 20 percent of $50, but the sale price is what remains, which is $50 minus $10, or $40.
ww.$45: The figure $45 would be a 10 percent discount, since $5 is 10 percent of $50, but a 20 percent discount removes $10 and leaves $40.

rw: Markup on cost equals the $10 profit divided by the $20 cost, which is 0.5 or 50 percent.

ww.33%: The figure 33% is the profit divided by the selling price, which is $10 over $30, but markup on cost divides by the $20 cost instead.
ww.150%: The figure 150% inverts the ratio by dividing the $30 price by the $20 cost, but markup is the extra $10 divided by the $20 cost.
ww.10%: The figure 10% takes the dollar profit of $10 as a percent without dividing by cost, but the right step is $10 divided by $20.

rw: In a sole proprietorship the owner and business are legally the same, so the owner is personally liable for debts and can lose personal assets.

ww.It is expensive to start for most owners: Sole proprietorships are usually cheap and easy to start with few legal steps, so being expensive to start is not a real disadvantage.
ww.It must share profits with shareholders: Sharing profits with shareholders applies to corporations, but a sole proprietor keeps all profits and has no shareholders, so this is not a disadvantage.
ww.The owner has no control over the firm: The owner has full control over the firm in a sole proprietorship, so having no control is false and describes the reverse of the truth.

rw: In a partnership, partners can combine money, skills and work, which gives the business more resources than a single owner would have.

ww.Partners never disagree on any matter: Partners can and do disagree at times, so saying they never disagree is unrealistic and is not a true advantage of a partnership.
ww.Partners have no duty for the debts of o: In a general partnership, partners are usually responsible for each other's business debts, so having no duty for them is false.
ww.Profits belong to one person only, the o: Profits belonging to one person only describes a sole proprietorship, whereas in a partnership the profits are shared among the partners.

rw: Partners can disagree about decisions, and in a general partnership each partner can be held liable for the actions of the others.

ww.It pays no taxes on any income that it e: Partnerships do not escape taxes on income, since profits are taxed through the partners, so claiming no taxes at all is false.
ww.Only one person decides for the firm and: Only one person deciding for the firm describes a sole proprietorship, since in a partnership decisions are shared among several partners.
ww.It cannot raise any money from banks or: Partnerships can raise money from banks and investors, and having several owners often helps, so saying they never can is wrong.

map.It has the fewest rules of all: It has the fewest rules of all business types

rw: This option is marked as the answer in the bank, but a corporation cannot replace skills in any field, so it is a flawed choice that does not make sense.

ww.It has the fewest rules of all business: Corporations face many legal and tax rules, such as filings and double taxation, so having the fewest rules of all business types is false.
ww.It guarantees you any job that you apply: A corporation cannot guarantee you any job, since hiring depends on employers and applicants, so this claim has nothing to do with a business structure.
ww.It avoids the need for a resume or a cov: Applying for jobs may still require a resume or cover letter, and a corporation has no power over that, so this option does not describe an advantage.

rw: Double taxation means a corporation pays tax on its profits, and then shareholders pay tax again on the dividends they receive from those profits.

ww.Paying a tax twice on one purchase, at t: Paying a tax twice on a single purchase is not what double taxation means, which refers to corporate profits being taxed at two levels.
ww.Filing two tax returns in a year, one fo: Filing two returns, one for the state and one for the nation, is about two governments and does not describe the same income taxed twice at the firm and owner level.
ww.Paying sales tax at two stores on goods: Paying sales tax at two stores on separate purchases is just buying in two places, and each sale is taxed once, so it is not double taxation.

rw: A stock is a share of ownership in a corporation, so stockholders own a small part of the company and may share in its profits.

ww.A type of insurance for firms and homes: Insurance protects against losses in exchange for a premium, and a stock is not a policy but a piece of a company.
ww.A loan to a company with interest paid: A loan to a company with interest paid describes a bond, since stockholders own part of the firm and are not lenders.
ww.A bank account held by a firm or a perso: A bank account holds deposits and does not give ownership in a company, whereas a stock does.

rw: A dividend is a share of a corporation's profits paid out to its shareholders, usually as cash on a regular schedule.

ww.A tax paid on income to the state each y: A tax paid on income by a firm is a corporate income tax, which goes to the government and is not paid out to shareholders.
ww.A price paid for goods at the till, show: A price paid for goods at the till is simply the purchase price, which has no link to profits paid to the owners of a company.
ww.A fee paid to a bank for use of an accou: A fee paid to a bank for an account is a service charge, which is a cost to the account holder, not a payout of profits.

rw: A cooperative is a business owned and run by its members for their shared benefit, with each member usually having a say and sharing in the gains.

ww.A business owned by the government and r: A business owned by the government for the public good is a state owned enterprise, while a cooperative is owned by its members instead.
ww.A business that competes with its member: A cooperative does not compete with its own members, since the members own it and use its goods or services together for their benefit.
ww.A business owned by one investor who run: A business owned by one investor who runs it alone is a sole proprietorship, whereas a cooperative has many owner members.

rw: A franchisee buys the right to run a business under another company's brand, paying fees and following its rules in return for its name and system.

ww.The company that owns the brand and lice: The company that owns the brand and licenses it is the franchisor, and the franchisee is the other party, who buys the right to run an outlet.
ww.A bank that lends to the brand and holds: A bank that lends to the brand is a lender, which may finance firms but does not buy the right to run an outlet, so it is not a franchisee.
ww.A customer of the brand who buys its goo: A customer who buys goods each week is a consumer of the brand, and does not run an outlet or hold rights, so this is not a franchisee.

rw: A franchise gives a proven business system and brand recognition, so the owner starts with customers and methods that already work, which lowers some risk.

ww.Freedom to change the brand, menu and pr: Freedom to change the brand, menu and prices at will is not allowed in a franchise, because the franchisor sets rules for all outlets to stay consistent.
ww.No fees to pay to the brand owner at all: Franchisees normally pay start up fees and ongoing royalties to the brand owner, so saying there are no fees is false.
ww.A guaranteed profit for the owner each y: No business can promise a guaranteed profit each year, and franchises can fail, so this claim is false despite the support a brand offers.

rw: A patent gives an inventor exclusive rights to an invention for a set time, which stops others from making or selling it without permission.

ww.A license to open a store, issued by the: A license to open a store is a business permit from the city, which allows a shop to operate and does not protect an invention.
ww.A right to a book that you wrote and sel: A right to a book that you wrote is a copyright, which protects creative works, while a patent protects inventions.
ww.A right to a brand name and to its logo: A right to a brand name and logo is a trademark, which identifies a company's goods, whereas a patent protects an invention.

rw: A trademark is a word, symbol or design that identifies a brand and keeps others from using a confusingly similar mark for their goods.

ww.A tax on a brand name and its logo each: A tax on a brand name is not what a trademark is, because a trademark is a form of legal protection and not a payment.
ww.A right to an invention granted for twen: A right to an invention for twenty years describes a patent, which protects inventions, whereas a trademark protects names and symbols.
ww.A right to a song that you wrote and sin: A right to a song you wrote is a copyright, which protects creative works, whereas a trademark protects brand identifiers.

rw: Copyright is legal protection for original creative works such as books, music and art, giving the creator control over how they are copied and used.

ww.Protection for trade secrets such as rec: Protection for trade secrets such as recipes comes from keeping the information private and from trade secret law, which is a different protection from copyright.
ww.Protection for brand names and logo mark: Protection for brand names and logo marks is a trademark, which identifies a company's goods, whereas copyright covers creative works.
ww.Protection for inventions and new device: Protection for inventions and new devices is a patent, which covers how something works, whereas copyright protects creative expression like writing and music.

rw: An original song is a creative work, and copyright gives its author legal protection and control over copying and performance of it.

ww.Trademark: A trademark protects brand names and logos, which identifies a seller's goods, so it does not fit an original song written by a student.
ww.Patent: A patent protects an invention or new device, whereas a song is a creative work and so a patent is the wrong protection for it.
ww.License: A license is permission to use something, such as a work or a right, and does not itself protect a song the student wrote.

rw: Insurance protects a business against financial loss, and in exchange the owner pays a premium, so the insurer covers certain damages if they occur.

ww.A loan for new equipment from a bank or: A loan for new equipment is financing from a lender that must be repaid, which is different from insurance that covers losses for a fee.
ww.A tax on property owned by a firm in a t: A tax on property is a charge set by a local government, whereas insurance is a private agreement that pays out for covered losses.
ww.A discount from suppliers given to a bus: A discount for buying in bulk is a supplier pricing term, which lowers cost per unit and does not protect a firm against loss.

rw: A premium is the amount paid for an insurance policy, usually monthly or yearly, in return for coverage against a loss.

ww.The amount you pay before coverage start: The amount you pay before coverage starts is the deductible, which is a different part of an insurance policy from the premium.
ww.The profit of the insurer on each policy: The insurer's profit on a policy is what remains after claims and costs, whereas the premium is what the customer pays to get coverage.
ww.The money paid out after a loss occurs: The money paid out after a loss is a claim payment or benefit, which goes to the policy holder, so it is not the premium.

rw: Insurance helps protect an owner against costly losses from events like fire or lawsuits, which could otherwise force the business to close.

ww.To guarantee profit for the business in: Insurance cannot guarantee profit, because it only covers certain losses, and a firm can still lose money from poor sales or high costs.
ww.To stop needing a business plan when see: Insurance does not replace a business plan, which banks and investors usually still want when deciding whether to give funds.
ww.To avoid all taxes that apply to the bus: Insurance does not remove taxes, because a business must still pay the taxes the law requires whether it holds insurance or not.

rw: A producer of raw materials grows or extracts basic materials, such as farm crops, timber or minerals, which other firms then use to make goods.

ww.A store that sells finished goods to cus: A store that sells finished goods to customers is a retailer, which sits later in the chain than a producer of raw materials.
ww.A firm that advises customers on how to: A firm that advises customers is a consulting or service business, which gives advice and does not grow or extract basic materials.
ww.A bank that lends money to firms and to: A bank lends money and provides financial services, which does not involve growing or extracting basic materials, so it is not a raw material producer.

rw: A financial service involves money, such as banking, loans or insurance, helping people and firms save, borrow, invest and protect against loss.

ww.A service that repairs cars and trucks f: Repairing cars and trucks is an automotive service that fixes vehicles, which does not mainly involve handling money, so it is not a financial service.
ww.A service that cuts hair for men, women: Cutting hair is a personal care service, which has to do with grooming people and not with managing money.
ww.A service that cleans offices each night: Cleaning offices is a maintenance service that keeps buildings tidy, and it does not involve managing money, so it is not a financial service.

rw: A bank is an institution that takes deposits from savers and makes loans to borrowers, earning money from the interest it charges.

ww.A company that prints newspapers and mag: A company that prints newspapers is a publisher or printer, whose work is producing media and not taking deposits or lending money.
ww.A store that sells only coins and stamps: A store that sells coins and stamps to collectors is a specialty shop for hobbyists and does not take deposits or make loans like a bank.
ww.A government tax office that collects ta: A tax office collects taxes for the government, whereas a bank is a business that holds customers' money and lends it out.

rw: Advertising is paid messages that promote a product to an audience, aiming to inform people and persuade them to buy.

ww.Making the product in a plant for sale t: Making a product in a plant is production or manufacturing, which creates the goods and does not promote them to buyers.
ww.Delivering the product to buyers by road: Delivering products by road or rail is distribution or shipping, which moves goods to buyers and does not promote them.
ww.Setting the price of a product to cover: Setting the price of a product to cover its costs is pricing, which is another part of marketing but not the same as advertising.

rw: Short videos on social media are where many teenagers spend time, so ads there reach the target audience in a place and style they use.

ww.Printed flyers in an office: Printed flyers in an office would mostly reach adults at work, and so they would miss teenagers, who spend their time in school and online.
ww.Radio ads at three at night: Radio ads at three at night would reach very few listeners, and teenagers are usually asleep then, so they would be missed.
ww.Ads in a retirement newsletter: Ads in a retirement newsletter would reach older readers, who are not the teenage audience, so this places the message in front of the wrong people.

rw: A target market is the group of customers a business aims to serve, chosen by traits like age, interests or needs.

ww.The business's competitors, who sell sim: The business's competitors are other firms selling similar goods, and they are rivals and not the customers the business wants to serve.
ww.Every person in the world, whoever they: Aiming at every person in the world is unrealistic, since a target market is a specific group, so this option is too broad.
ww.The business's employees and their famil: Employees and their families are the firm's workforce, and they are not the customer group that the business chooses to serve.

rw: Market research is gathering information about customers and competitors, so a business can decide what to sell, to whom and at what price.

ww.Making products in a factory for the sho: Making products in a factory is manufacturing, which produces goods and does not gather information about the market.
ww.Printing flyers to hand out in the stree: Printing flyers to hand out is a form of advertising that promotes products, and it does not gather information.
ww.Filing taxes with the state each year by: Filing taxes with the state is a legal and accounting duty, and it does not collect information about customers or competitors.

rw: A survey is a set of questions asked to collect opinions or information from people, which businesses use to learn what customers want.

ww.A legal contract signed by two firms tha: A legal contract signed by two firms is an agreement between parties and not a tool for collecting opinions, so it is not a survey.
ww.A record of sales kept by the firm for e: A record of sales kept by the firm is a sales report, which tracks what was sold and does not gather opinions through questions.
ww.A list of company products with their pr: A list of products with prices shown to buyers is a catalog or price list, and it does not ask people questions.

rw: Inventory is the goods a business holds for sale or for making products, such as stock on shelves or materials waiting in a storeroom.

ww.Employees assigned to a task, as listed: Employees assigned to a task are a staffing roster, which is about people and their time and not about goods held by the business.
ww.Profit earned in a year by the firm and: Profit earned in a year is income, which is a financial result and not the physical goods that a business holds.
ww.Money owed to a business by customers wh: Money owed to a business by customers is accounts receivable, which is a financial asset and not the goods a firm holds for sale.

rw: Overordering a seasonal item leaves unsold stock after the season ends, which ties up the store's money in goods that cannot be sold at full price.

ww.More customers than the store needs: Having more customers than needed is not a problem caused by overordering, since ordering too much leaves extra goods and does not bring extra shoppers.
ww.Lower storage costs for the store: Ordering too much raises storage costs and does not lower them, since more stock takes more space and care.
ww.Higher profit for sure on all items: Extra stock does not guarantee profit, since unsold goods may need to be discounted or thrown away, so higher profit for sure is wrong.

rw: Shipping is moving goods from one place to another, such as from a factory to a warehouse or from a seller to a buyer.

ww.Advertising goods to buyers online: Advertising goods to buyers online is a promotion activity, which spreads awareness and does not physically move products.
ww.Making goods in a plant from raw materia: Making goods in a plant from raw materials is manufacturing, which creates the products and does not move them to buyers.
ww.Counting goods in the stockroom daily: Counting goods in the stockroom is inventory control, which tracks stock on hand and does not move it between places.

rw: A vendor is a seller of goods or services, such as a supplier who sells products to a store or to the public.

ww.A buyer of goods and services: A buyer of goods and services is a customer or consumer, and this is the opposite side of a vendor, who sells.
ww.A manager of a store or shop: A manager of a store runs daily operations and supervises staff, which is a different role from a vendor who sells goods.
ww.A worker who repairs machines: A worker who repairs machines is a technician, whose job is maintenance, and this is not the same as a seller of goods.

rw: Technology helps businesses work faster, reach more customers and manage information, through tools like software, websites and databases that save time and effort.

ww.Replacing all employees with machines, s: Replacing all employees is not technology's role, since firms still need people, so the idea that no people are paid is an exaggeration.
ww.Removing the need for customers by makin: Technology does not remove the need for customers, and products do not sell by magic, since every business still depends on buyers.
ww.Guaranteeing profit for every firm that: Buying a computer or phone cannot guarantee profit, because results depend on how the tool is used, so this claim is false.

rw: This option is marked as the answer in the bank, but learning only in high school does not show a business using technology, so it is a flawed choice.

ww.Learning only from books and from printe: Learning only from books and printed texts is a way of studying and is not a business using technology to improve service.
ww.A restaurant removing its phone so peopl: Removing the phone makes it harder for customers to reach the restaurant, so this lowers service quality and uses no technology to improve it.
ww.Avoiding new skills and sticking to what: Avoiding new skills and staying with old methods shows no use of technology and would not improve service, so this fails as an example.

rw: Global business operates or trades across countries, such as firms that import, export or run offices and factories in several nations.

ww.Business done only in one town, with no: Business done only in one town with no trade abroad is local business, which is the opposite of global business.
ww.Business done only online by one company: Business done only online in one city can still be local in reach, because global business means trading across countries, not just using the internet.
ww.Business done without customers or buyer: Business with no customers or buyers cannot earn revenue, so it cannot be a type of business, let alone global business.

rw: A tariff is a tax on imported goods, which raises their price and is often used to protect domestic producers from foreign competition.

ww.A discount on imports: A discount on imports would make foreign goods cheaper, whereas a tariff adds a tax that makes imported goods cost more.
ww.A tax on exports alone: A tax on exports alone describes an export duty, which is different, since a tariff applies to goods coming into a country.
ww.A ban on trade in goods: A ban on trade in goods is an embargo or import ban, which stops trade completely, whereas a tariff only taxes the goods.

rw: A job is work you do regularly to earn pay, usually for an employer, which separates it from volunteering or a hobby.

ww.A volunteer role with no pay at all: A volunteer role with no pay at all is unpaid work, and a job is work you do to earn pay, so this does not fit.
ww.A hobby done for fun at home daily: A hobby done for fun at home is a leisure activity done without pay, and so it differs from a job that earns income.
ww.A lifelong series of work experiences: A lifelong series of work experiences is a career, which spans many positions, whereas a job is a single position.

rw: A job is one position, whereas a career is a long term path of work that can include many jobs, often in a related field.

ww.A career is unpaid, while a job is paid: A career is not unpaid, because it consists of paid work over a lifetime, so this reverses the true difference between the two.
ww.A job lasts for life, while a career las: A job does not last for life and a career does not last a day, so this has the two terms reversed.
ww.They mean exactly the same thing in all: The terms do not mean the same, since a job is one position and a career covers a long path, so saying they are identical is false.

rw: A values based career choice means choosing work that fits what matters most to you, such as helping others, security or creativity, which supports lasting satisfaction.

ww.Choosing the job with the shortest title: Picking the job with the shortest title ignores what you care about, and title length is a meaningless basis for a career choice.
ww.Choosing the first job offered to you in: Taking the first job offered is a choice of convenience, which may not reflect what matters to you, so it is not values based.
ww.Choosing a job at random from a list of: Choosing at random ignores your values altogether, and it is the opposite of a deliberate choice built on what matters to you.

rw: Knowing your strengths helps you choose careers where those strengths matter, so you are more likely to do well and enjoy the work.

ww.It guarantees a job in any field that yo: Knowing strengths cannot guarantee a job in any field, since hiring depends on many factors, so the word guarantee makes this false.
ww.It removes the need to learn new skills: Knowing your strengths does not remove the need to learn new skills at work, since careers keep changing and require ongoing learning.
ww.It lets you avoid all of your weaknesses: Knowing strengths does not let you avoid all weaknesses, since everyone has some, and you often still need to work on them.

rw: An aptitude is a natural ability or talent for something, which can point you toward careers where you may learn quickly and do well.

ww.A salary level paid by a firm to staff: A salary level is the pay a firm offers for a role, which is set by the employer and is not a natural talent.
ww.A required degree that a worker must hol: A required degree is an education credential that a role may demand, and it is learned, not a natural ability.
ww.A job title printed on a business card: A job title printed on a business card is a label for a position, and it says nothing about a person's natural ability.

rw: An occupation outlook is a forecast of how many jobs will be available in a field, helping people decide which careers may offer good openings.

ww.A salary history listing the pay of your: A salary history lists the pay of your past jobs and looks backward, whereas an outlook looks ahead at future job availability.
ww.A list of past jobs and the dates that y: A list of past jobs and the dates you held them is a work history on a resume, which looks backward and does not forecast demand.
ww.A view from a window at work, showing th: A view from a window at work is a literal sight and not a career term, so it has no connection to forecasting job openings.

rw: The Occupational Outlook Handbook from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics gives researched data on job growth, pay and training, so it is a reliable source.

ww.An advertisement for a job or a firm in: An advertisement is written to sell a product or fill a job, so it may be biased and does not give reliable data on job growth and pay.
ww.A rumor from a classmate who heard it fr: A rumor from a classmate is secondhand and unchecked, so it is unreliable for judging job growth or pay compared with official data.
ww.An anonymous social media post that clai: An anonymous social media post cannot be verified and may be wrong, so it is a weak source for facts about pay and job growth.

rw: A mentor is an experienced person who guides someone with less experience, giving advice, feedback and support to help them grow in their career.

ww.A person who hires employees for a firm: A person who hires employees is a recruiter or hiring manager, who decides who joins the firm, and that role is different from a mentor.
ww.A person who sells products to buyers in: A person who sells products to buyers is a salesperson, who works in commerce and does not necessarily guide someone's growth.
ww.A person who repairs equipment in a fact: A person who repairs equipment is a technician, whose job is maintenance, and this role does not involve guiding someone with less experience.

rw: A portfolio in career planning is a collection of your work samples and achievements, which you can show employers as proof of your skills.

ww.A list of stocks you own in a firm or in: A list of stocks you own is an investment portfolio, which is a financial meaning of the word and not the career planning meaning.
ww.A record of your spending kept in a book: A record of your spending is a budget or expense log, which tracks money and does not show an employer samples of your work.
ww.A bag for carrying papers to work, with: A bag for carrying papers to work is a briefcase, and although it shares the word with portfolio, it does not show your work or achievements.
